title: CHAPTER SIX. On Sacred Scripture's clarity
english:
CHAPTER SIX
On Sacred Scripture's clarity

So far concerning Sacred Scripture's perfection and sufficiency: next comes clarity. Clarity is Scripture's property by which everything that holds the faith and the manners of living is so openly set down in it, and so found there, that God-fearers — using proper means with careful effort and wisdom, guided by God, and giving no credit to themselves or their own reasoningn's age, know it surely and understand it unto salvation.

title: Catholic ASSERTIO: saving dogmas are plain and open; Hilary; against the idle and malicious
english: Our assertion — and it is Augustine's own, and indeed the catholic one — is this: the truth of the sentences of the faith, in dogmas supernaturally revealed and necessary to be known and believed unto salvation, stands plain and open. No one can ignore or deny those dogmas except the idle toward inquiry or the malicious toward contradiction. As Hilary says, God does not lead us to the blessed life through hard questions.

title: Reasons 1–3: Scripture's own witness; internal lamp; Christ's promise of the Spirit
english: The reasons are these.

1. From Scripture's own testimony ([[Deuteronomy 30:11 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 30:11]]–[[Deuteronomy 30:14 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 30:14]]): that place does not speak of the ease of keeping the law, but of the ease of understanding it — which, with Alfonso Tostado Bishop of Avila, Bellarmine himself (On grace and free will book 3 chapter 6) proves and confesses to seem the most literal and proper reading. And what Moses said here of Old Testament doctrine Paul applies to the dogmas of the New Testament ([[Romans 10:6 >> Bible:Romans 10:6]] and following).

2. From Scripture's inward property, by which it is called a lamp to our feet ([[Psalm 119:105 >> Bible:Psalm 119:105]]), a lamp shining in a dark place ([[2 Peter 1:19 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:19]]); add [[Psalm 19:4 >> Bible:Psalm 19:4]]–[[Psalm 19:9 >> Bible:Psalm 19:9]], [[Psalm 19:12 >> Bible:Psalm 19:12]].

3. From Christ's promise ([[John 16:12 >> Bible:John 16:12]]-[[John 16:13 >> Bible:John 16:13]]): "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will lead you into all the truth; for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come." Likewise [[1 John 2:27 >> Bible:1 John 2:27]]: "The anointing teaches you concerning all things, and is true and is not a lie; and as it taught you, you will remain in him." By this it is signified that we are most fully instructed in the things needful to salvation — which is wrongly dragged to bishops gathered in a council as if they were infallible, of whom Bellarmine (On the authority of councils book 2 chapter 2) confesses that, existing apart, they are not taught every truth by the Holy Spirit.

title: Reasons 4–7: Christ's command to search; Bereans; fathers; Scripture's end
english: 4. From Christ's precept: why would he bid us search the Scriptures ([[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]]) if they could not be understood?
5. From the example of the primitive Church that obeyed this precept ([[Acts 17:11 >> Bible:Acts 17:11]]).

6. From the example of the ancient fathers, who prove the articles of the faith from Scripture. Hence Constantine in the Nicene synod: "Let us dissolve the matters brought into question by the testimonies of the divinely inspired letters." Things brought into question are ambiguous and obscure. If therefore Scripture were equally ambiguous and obscure, those proofs and dissolutions would be ridiculous.
7. From Sacred Scripture's end, which is our teaching ([[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]), to which obscurity is diametrically opposed.

title: Reasons 8–9: from God who reveals; from prophets and Apostles as God's scribes
english: 8. From God's side as Revealer. Either God could speak perspicuously, short of unavoidable obscurity, or he could not. If you say he could not, you speak falsely, because nothing here impedes his power ([[Exodus 4:11 >> Bible:Exodus 4:11]]; Lactantius, Institutes book 6 chapter 21). Therefore he could. If he could, either he ought to speak perspicuously, or he ought not. That he ought not is hardly granted by his wisdom and goodness. If he ought, either he willed it, or he did not. That he did not is absurd, and it cries out against sacred Scripture's sayings and aim ([[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]; [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]; [[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]]; [[2 Peter 1:19 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:19]]). Therefore he willed it, and accordingly he spoke clearly — by the argument of [[Psalm 115:3 >> Bible:Psalm 115:3]].

9. From God's scribes — the prophets and Apostles. Either they could write clearly, or they could not. The latter is absurd, because those who before were rude and unlettered became lettered ([[Acts 4:13 >> Bible:Acts 4:13]]), and soon, moved by God's Spirit, spoke ([[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]), knowing every tongue that was under heaven ([[Acts 2:8 >> Bible:Acts 2:8]] and following). If they could, either they ought, or they ought not. That they ought not, the prophetic office and the apostleship do not permit ([[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]; [[John 20:31 >> Bible:John 20:31]]; [[1 John 2:3 >> Bible:1 John 2:3]]); hence they are called the light of the world ([[Matthew 5:14 >> Bible:Matthew 5:14]]; [[Acts 13:46 >> Bible:Acts 13:46]]). If they ought, either they willed, or they refused. Not the latter — by the argument of [[Acts 4:20 >> Bible:Acts 4:20]]. Therefore they willed, and accordingly they wrote with the sun's ray, however much Scripture-shunners deny it — as Tertullian (On the resurrection of the flesh chapter 47) names such people.

title: Reasons 10–11: revealed dogmas can be taught clearly; papists admit it; simple style
english: 10. From the side of revealed dogmas. Either they could be handed down perspicuously, or they could not. If you assert the latter, you err, because — by the papists' own witnesses — certain things, and indeed those needful to all for salvation, are written so clearly that they can be understood by the pious and industrious. Thomas (Summa Theologiae part 1 question 1 article 9 reply to objection 2): "Those things which in one place of Scripture are said under metaphors are set out more expressly in other places." Costerus (Enchiridion chapter 1): "We do not deny that those chief heads of the faith which are needful for all Christians to know unto salvation are comprehended perspicuously enough in the Apostolic writings." And Gregory of Valencia (Analysis of the faith book 3): "Those truths of the faith which absolutely and simply must necessarily be known and believed by all human beings are truly taught perspicuously in the Scriptures" — as Augustine also noted.
11. From the side of style. For it is simple, open, and most fitting for expressing such great mysteries ([[1 Corinthians 2:1 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:1]] and following).

title: II. Partial obscurity admitted; human causes; hard places in Paul; Spirit's wise mixture
english: II. Next, we do not deny that Sacred Scripture is in some part, somewhere, and for someone obscure — whether we look at sublime matters full of mysteries, or at phrases proper to that ancient time, and also tropic and figured locutions that in this age make some difficulty for us.

That obscurity is increased by human prejudices, ignorance of tongues and of things, vain confidence, negligence, hatred, envy, ambition, avarice, lust of wrangling, and every depraved affection by which the mind is blinded.

Hence Peter also ([[2 Peter 3:16 >> Bible:2 Peter 3:16]]), concerning Paul's letters, affirms that they contain some things hard to understand (some things difficult to grasp) — to tame pride by labor, and to remove the intellect from distaste, for what is easily investigated often becomes cheap to it.

For magnificently and wholesomely the Holy Spirit so shaped the Scriptures that by the clearer places he meets hunger, and by the obscurer ones he wipes away distaste — as Augustine wisely writes (On Christian Doctrine book 2 chapter 6).

title: Six reasons God willed some obscurity; Flacius; Augustine; Constantine at Nicaea
english: We therefore distinctly set out several reasons for this assertion.
1. Because God willed that there should be cause to say with David: "Give me understanding, and I will search your law" ([[Psalm 119:34 >> Bible:Psalm 119:34]]).
2. That human arrogance might be beaten back.
3. That distaste might be removed.
4. That our diligence might be stirred.
5. That Sacred Scripture itself might be held in greater price — which Theodoret in the preface to Ezekiel declares by various examples.

6. That a keener desire for the other life might be kindled in us, where we will no longer know in part and prophesy in part, but what is imperfect will be done away, and we will see face to face, not through a mirror or in a riddle ([[1 Corinthians 13:9 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:9]] and following).

Consult Flacius Illyricus, Clavis part 2 treatise 1 on the way of knowing the sacred letters. Wisely Augustine adds to the words cited above: "Almost nothing is drawn from those obscurities that is not found said most clearly elsewhere." Before all things, therefore, one must be turned by the fear of God to knowing his will. And in the same book chapter 9: to illustrate obscurer locutions, examples are to be taken from the clearer ones, and the testimonies of certain sentences are to remove doubt about the uncertain.

Here also belongs the law of Constantine the Great in Theodoret (Church History book 1), passed with the votes of three hundred eighteen bishops in the Nicene council: the Evangelical and Apostolic books and the oracles of the ancient prophets perspicuously instruct us in the sense of the Deity — that is, what we ought to think about God and divine things. Therefore, hostile discord laid aside, let us take from the divinely inspired Scriptures the solution and decision of the controversies that are to be handled.

title: III. Not absolute but conditioned and sufficient perspicuity for canonical teaching
english: III. We therefore do not assert an absolute and every-way perspicuity of the Scriptures handed down to us, but a conditioned and sufficient one for discharging the canonical and didactic office for those who read and search them decently.

This is shown from [[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]] and [[Psalm 19:12 >> Bible:Psalm 19:12]]. For here are all things needful, clear, and straight — all necessary, clear, manifest, and right — Chrysostom witnessing (volume 3 on 2 Thessalonians); not needing explanation but only hearing — Justin Martyr witnessing (Dialogue with Trypho). Yet diligent scrutiny and meditation are needed so that they become perspicuous to the reader, according to Cyril of Alexandria (Against Julian book 9): "Nothing is hard for those who dwell in the Scriptures as they ought." And Clement of Alexandria (Stromata book 7): one must examine the Scriptures accurately, not read them casually. And Epiphanius (Against heresies): all things are clear in the divine Scripture for those who wish to approach the divine word with pious reasoning.

title: Obscurities conquerable for the pious cautious reader; Lambert; Scripture alone God's certain testimony; Cap. 6 close
english: Obscurities, therefore, if any seem to be present, are conquerable when the means are applied, for the pious and cautious reader.

Rightly Francis Lambert, once professor at Marburg, teaches that Sacred Scripture is opened to those who attribute nothing to themselves and to their own judgment. Likewise: if you possess wit, learning, and experience, renounce these when you come to Christ's school. Renounce them, I say — not that you wholly refuse them, but that you trust nothing to them: otherwise you will not be a fit disciple of Christ, and he will neither teach you nor open Scripture's most longed-for door.
For of God's truth and will Scripture alone is the certain and infallible testimony.
